recent.text: Hobb Ashcombe says: "Fair's fair, clock. No thirteen tonight."

Hobb Ashcombe wedged an iron poker between the teeth of the Great Gear, and the poker shrieked and held. The tower's wheels groaned and stopped, and the ticking that had run through Wumbleby all night went out of the air. The clock's hands stood still a whisker short of midnight. In Gloomer's Meadow the humming lullaby jammed on a single note and hung there. Down Crooked Lane, the shadows that had been trotting toward the meadow turned and came tumbling back uphill toward the houses.

Hobb set his feet in the Gearloft, jammed an iron poker between the teeth of the Great Gear and heaved it home with all his weight. The gear shrieked and stopped, and the whole tower went silent. He told the clock, "Fair's fair, clock. No thirteen tonight."

I clutch my shawl and peek at Hobb, then at the poker wedged in the great gear. "Goodness, Hobb, that was dramatic! Is it truly stopped? Because the shadows are tumbling back uphill, and I'd like to run down and see whether the children are waking." If he's willing, I'll go down the stairs to the Tock Tower and out to the square to look for Pip.

The clock has stopped and the shadows are heading home, so I want to see with my own eyes that the children wake. Maybe somebody will notice I was there when it happened, and I'd like Pip to know it's done.

You clutch your shawl and peek at Hobb, then at the iron poker wedged deep between the Great Gear's teeth. The wheels strain and creak and stay put, and the clock's hands sit frozen a whisker before midnight.

Marigold: "Goodness, Hobb, that was dramatic! Is it truly stopped? Because the shadows are tumbling back uphill, and I'd like to run down and see whether the children are waking."

The yellow glow from the clock face falls across Hobb's shoulders. The ladder waits by the wall, leading down into the silent tower. Hobb has heard you, and the quiet in the Gearloft waits for his answer.

Dilly swings the pole off his shoulder, grins at Mags Ragwort, and says, "Right, chum, the Tock Tower's the trouble. Hobb's poker's jammed the Great Gear, and I've fixed a hundred gears easier than that, easy as winking. Come with me, and mind the fog on Tock Lane. I'll have the tower ticking again before the moon moves an inch."

The clock stopped a whisker short of midnight, and the shadows are running back uphill because of it, so I think the Great Gear is the key to all of this. I want to be the one who frees the tower's wheels and gets the ticking going again, so that everyone in Wumbleby knows Dilly Quickstep did it.

You swing the lamplighter's pole off your shoulder and grin at the old woman by the cart.

Dilly: "Right, chum, the Tock Tower's the trouble. Hobb's poker's jammed the Great Gear, and I've fixed a hundred gears easier than that, easy as winking. Come with me, and mind the fog on Tock Lane. I'll have the tower ticking again before the moon moves an inch."

Mags: She sucks her teeth and goes on feeding the donkey a peppermint. "Not me, petal. I'll mind me cart. Go on, then."

You go north, and the square's slanting cobbles give way to the tower's round bottom room. The chains hang still, and the silence is so big it hums. The smell of oil is thick, and the cot, the kettle and the cluttered workbench crowd the wall where old Ambrose Tock lives. He keeps looking up at the ceiling and chuckling. Overhead, the ladder climbs through the hole into the gearloft, and the south door lets back out onto the square.

Ambrose is right beside you, still chuckling at the ceiling. What do you do?

recent.text: I stride halfway down the lane to the drain the grown-ups won't talk about, crouch over the grate with my goggles pulled down, and hold my notebook open in the moonlight. "Hypothesis: the drain knows something. Test: ask it politely, and if that fails, be ruder." I lean in close and listen.

Three days of sleeping children with no shadows, and the whole town shrugs. That's the sort of silence a drain keeps too. If something's moving under Wumbleby, I want to hear it before I go anywhere near that peddler's wagon in the meadow.

You walk halfway down Crooked Lane, from one thin pool of lamplight into the dark and out again, until the round iron grating sits at your feet in the gutter. Fog curls around your boots. You crouch, pull your goggles down, and hold your notebook open in the light of the fat orange moon.

"Hypothesis: the drain knows something. Test: ask it politely, and if that fails, be ruder," you say, and lean in close to listen.

Up through the smile-shaped holes comes a soft wet sound, patient, like someone licking their lips. Then a whisper, in rhyme: "Down in the dark where the drippings drain, who will answer me, once again?"

When your words have faded, the whisper only giggles, "Again and again!", and goes back to its licking. Behind you, a small shadow with nobody to cast it slips over the cobbles and trots on downhill. The grating gurgles softly, waiting.
